agree.reason: The candid A1C section, the no-contract terms and the $59 call-plus-meals trial give a wary, burned-before reader a low-risk reason to click, though nothing speaks directly to why this attempt would last when the others didn't.

honest.reason: The page drops the requested 'will lower your A1C' claim, reports the 10/3/1 split and the 0.6 average accurately, names the small self-selected sample and the untracked medication changes, and invents nothing.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 a meal but leaves several favourable true figures unstated: the trial at about $5.90 a meal, 37 of 88 as more than 4 in 10 staying past six months, and 10 of 14 as about 7 in 10.

right_comparison.reason: The alternative is only touched on with 'every meal means counting carbs', with no concrete picture of cooking and counting yourself, what that costs, or the apps this reader already quit.

qualification.reason: The hedge honestly names the small sample, the self-selection and the medication blind spot, but it gives the reader nothing checkable, such as rechecking A1C with their doctor at three months and what to do if it hasn't moved.

objections.reason: Cost, commitment, food boredom and health hype are each met with facts (trial week, no contract, swaps, honest numbers, retention), but the reader's main worry, quitting within two months, is answered only indirectly by the six-month figure.

fit.reason: It is a sales page of about 400 words with clear sections and a repeated order button, as the brief asked, and it swaps the overreaching A1C claim for one the facts support, which the client accepts.
